passage:
After his cousin died in an accident, Akash sat in his room asking why God had allowed it. Prayer felt like talking into an empty cup. He was furious too, since his cousin had done nothing to deserve it. He wrote a page to God, full of harsh words, and kept it in his diary. An old prayer he found later held protest of its own.

At the next gathering, some people went cold when he asked a question about suffering, and a few stopped saying hello. He felt lonely. But Minakshi, an elder who ran the youth group, said, "Doubt is not the end of belief. Ask, and read." She lent him two books on how different traditions wrestle with loss. He also found a classmate, Damini, who did not share his faith and simply listened.

At home his parents grew anxious. "Are you leaving us?" his mother asked. Akash said, "I love you. I ask because I take it seriously." He did not mock the family prayers. He sat with them and stayed quiet during the chant. Over the weeks he shared one small question at a time. His father nodded. "We can think about it together."

qa.a: She lent him two books on how different traditions wrestle with loss.

qa.q: How did the faith community's reaction to Akash's questions differ from his parents', and what helped him?
qa.a: The community went cold and left him lonely, while his parents were afraid he was leaving them. Minakshi welcomed the doubt and lent books, and with his parents he reassured them of his love and shared one small question at a time.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling toward God after his cousin died?
qa.a: He felt furious and empty, since prayer felt like talking into an empty cup.

qa.q: What did Akash do with his anger at God?
qa.a: He wrote a page to God full of harsh words and kept it in his diary, instead of holding it in.

grounding: After a loss, one young man doubts and rages at God, meets a cold response from some in his community, and works through his parents' fear with an open elder's help.
